implementation_notes: The try-with-resources statement declares resources that implement java.lang.AutoCloseable (all java.io.Closeable types qualify) and closes them in the reverse order of declaration when the block completes, normally or abruptly; if the body and a close both throw, the close exception is suppressed behind the body's exception and can be retrieved with Throwable.getSuppressed(). For actions that are not resources - rollback, restore state, end a span - the substitute is try/finally, optionally with a small AutoCloseable holder if the action must compose with other resources; the classic guard object survives only where the same release action has to be handed to a framework or shared across classes.
pitfalls: Only AutoCloseable instances may be declared in the resource list: a plain cleanup action needs try/finally or an explicit wrapper, otherwise the guard does not exist at all.
A suppressed close exception is easy to lose because callers only see the primary exception - inspect getSuppressed() (or log inside close()) or the cleanup failure disappears.

Anything opened before the try is not managed: the tutorial's own finally-based FileReader/BufferedReader example leaks the reader if the second open fails, so owned resources belong in the header, not before it.
